chain.g: to bear; (reflexive) bear oneself, behave, act

ety.text: From Medieval Latin gestūra (“a mode of action”), from Latin gerō (“to bear; (reflexive) bear oneself, behave, act”), past participle gestus. By surface analysis, Latin gest- + -ure.

senses.d: A motion of the limbs or body, especially one made to emphasize speech.
ex: The middle-finger gesture is really a nonverbal swear.
Grace was in all her steps, heaven in her eye, / In every gesture dignity and love.

senses.d: An act or a remark that serves as a formality or as a sign of attitude.
ex: We took flowers as a gesture of sympathy.
But, with a gesture, she put a period to this dalliance—one shouldn't palter so on an empty stomach, she might almost have said.

senses.d: A motion made with a pointing device, or on a touchscreen, that is recognised by the system as a command.
ex: This Web browser can be controlled with mouse gestures.

senses.d: The manner of carrying the body; position of the body or limbs; posture.
ex: Accubation, or lying down at meals, was a gesture used by very many nations.

senses.d: To make a gesture or gestures.
ex: My dad told me never to gesture with my hands when I talk.
Never gesture at someone using your middle finger: it may be perceived as an insult.

senses.d: To express (something) by a gesture or gestures.
To accompany or illustrate with gesture or action.
ex: It is not orderly read, nor gestured as beseemeth.

senses.d: To express or signal (to someone) by a gesture or gestures (to do something, go somewhere, etc).

pt:sinal.gl: sign; mark; trace (a visible or otherwise perceivable indication of something)

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese sinal, synal, from Late Latin signālis, from Latin signum. By surface analysis, sino + -al. Cognate with Spanish señal f, French signal m, and English signal.
